title: Inheritance
summary: The is-a relationship, method resolution, and where inheritance quietly turns fragile — overriding, super, multiple inheritance, and the diamond problem.

slides.markdown:
**Inheritance** lets a class reuse another class's fields and methods by declaring an **is-a** relationship — a `Car` is a `Vehicle`. Done well, it removes duplication; done carelessly, it's the most common source of tightly-coupled, fragile OOP designs.

This topic covers how method resolution actually works (overriding, `super`, hierarchies), why several languages restrict multiple inheritance, and the fragile base class problem that shows up once a hierarchy gets deep.

slides.sectionTitle: Inheritance: the is-a relationship and code reuse through a base class
slides.markdown:
**Inheritance** lets a class (the **subclass**/derived class) acquire the fields and methods of another class (the **base**/parent class), on the premise that the subclass genuinely **is a** kind of the base class. `class Car extends Vehicle` should read as "every Car is a Vehicle" — not just "Car wants Vehicle's code."

The reuse payoff is real: put `startEngine()`, `fuelLevel`, and `stop()` once on `Vehicle`, and `Car`, `Truck`, and `Motorcycle` all get them for free, each only adding what makes it distinct.

The is-a test is what keeps inheritance honest: if you can't honestly say "a Truck is a Vehicle" — as opposed to "a Truck happens to use some Vehicle code" — you're reaching for inheritance to solve a code-reuse problem that composition (a later topic) usually solves more safely.

**Overriding** replaces a base class's instance method with a subclass's version, and the replacement is resolved at runtime based on the object's actual type — call `vehicle.stop()` where `vehicle` is declared as `Vehicle` but actually holds a `Car`, and `Car`'s `stop()` runs.

**Hiding** (or shadowing) looks similar but applies to `static` methods and fields: a subclass declaring a `static` method with the same signature doesn't override it, it just adds a separate one, resolved at *compile time* based on the declared type, not the actual object. Call a hidden static method through a `Vehicle`-typed reference and you get `Vehicle`'s version even if the object is a `Car` — the opposite of overriding's behavior.

The interview trap: assuming `static` methods participate in polymorphism the same way instance methods do — they don't, because there's no `this` to dispatch on.

slides.sectionTitle: `super` calls: extending vs replacing base behavior
slides.markdown:
`super` lets an overriding method reach back and call the base class's version explicitly. Without it, an override **replaces** the base behavior entirely; with `super.methodName()` inside the override, you **extend** it — run the base logic, then add subclass-specific work on top.

A common pattern: `Car.stop()` calls `super.stop()` first (shut off the engine — shared Vehicle behavior) and then does Car-specific cleanup (retract the antenna). Skip the `super` call and you silently lose whatever the base class was doing, which is a frequent source of bugs when a shared setup or teardown step gets forgotten by a new override.

The rule of thumb: reach for `super` whenever the override should add to base behavior; skip it only when the subclass has a deliberate, complete reason to behave differently from scratch.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a class hierarchy and which method resolves where
slides.markdown:
In a hierarchy `Vehicle → Car → SportsCar`, calling `stop()` on a `SportsCar` object resolves by walking up from the object's actual class: if `SportsCar` overrides `stop()`, that version runs; if it doesn't, the search continues to `Car`, then to `Vehicle`, using the first override found.

This lookup — sometimes called dynamic dispatch — happens regardless of the variable's declared type; a `Vehicle v = new SportsCar()` still resolves to `SportsCar`'s override if one exists, because resolution is based on the object's real class, not the reference type.

slides.sectionTitle: Single vs multiple inheritance, and why many languages ban the latter
slides.markdown:
**Single inheritance** means a class extends exactly one base class. **Multiple inheritance** means a class can extend more than one — inheriting fields and methods from several parents at once. C++ allows it directly; Java, C#, and most modern languages ban inheriting from multiple *classes*, though they allow implementing multiple *interfaces* (which carry no state, side-stepping the worst problems).

The reason for the ban is concrete, not stylistic: if `Duck` extends both `FlyingAnimal` and `SwimmingAnimal`, and both base classes define a method with the same signature, which one does `Duck` inherit — and if both extend a common `Animal` ancestor, does `Duck` get one copy of `Animal`'s state or two? These aren't edge cases; they're the default outcome of allowing multiple class parents, and different languages have picked incompatible answers.

The next slide works through the sharpest version of this: the diamond problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the diamond problem, worked through
slides.markdown:
The **diamond problem**: `Animal` is the top of a diamond, `FlyingAnimal` and `SwimmingAnimal` both extend `Animal`, and `Duck` extends both `FlyingAnimal` and `SwimmingAnimal`. If `Animal` defines `move()` and neither middle class overrides it, does `Duck` inherit one `move()` or an ambiguous pair — and does `Duck` end up with one copy of `Animal`'s fields, or two independently-initialized copies (one via each parent path)?

C++ answers this with **virtual inheritance**, letting the diamond's base be shared explicitly instead of duplicated. Java and C# sidestep it entirely by banning multiple class inheritance, allowing the same shape only through interfaces, which carry no fields to duplicate in the first place.

![Diamond hierarchy with Duck inheriting from FlyingAnimal and SwimmingAnimal, both from Animal, marked with a question mark](assets/diamond-problem.svg)

slides.sectionTitle: Constructors in a hierarchy: initialization order base-to-derived
slides.markdown:
Constructing a `SportsCar` also constructs the `Car` and `Vehicle` inside it — and the order is fixed: the base class constructor always runs **before** the subclass constructor's own body, base-to-derived, regardless of which order you might expect. `new SportsCar()` runs `Vehicle()`, then `Car()`, then finally `SportsCar()`'s own body.

This exists because a subclass constructor's body may rely on base-class fields already being initialized — you can't safely set up `Car`-specific state before `Vehicle`'s fields exist. Most languages enforce this by implicitly (or explicitly, via `super(...)`) calling the base constructor as the very first line of a derived constructor.

The practical trap: a base constructor that calls an overridable method sees the *subclass's* override running before the subclass's own fields are initialized — a specific pitfall covered under Polymorphism.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: overriding a method and calling `super` for shared setup
Pitfall: the fragile base class problem — a base class change silently breaks subclasses
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This base class's internals are private — I can change how a method works internally without worrying about anything that extends it."

**Why it's wrong:** subclasses can depend on a base class's *behavior*, not just its public signature — if `Vehicle.refuel()` used to call `checkTank()` once and a subclass overrode `checkTank()` expecting exactly one call, changing `refuel()` to call `checkTank()` twice (a seemingly internal tweak) silently breaks every subclass relying on the old call count. The base class author often has no visibility into which subclasses exist or what they assumed.

**Correct model:** treat a base class's overridable methods, and the order/frequency in which it calls other overridable methods, as part of its public contract — changing that contract is a breaking change even if the field-level API looks untouched. This is one of the strongest real-world arguments for "favor composition over inheritance," covered in the next topic: composition doesn't expose this hidden surface at all.
